activities.model: A base case is the smallest version of the problem, answered directly (fact(1) is 1). Without one, or if each call doesn't get closer to it, the function keeps calling itself until Python runs out of stack and raises a RecursionError. fact(3) can't finish until fact(2) does, which waits on fact(1). Each waiting call keeps its own n in its own box on the call stack. fact(1) answers 1, then fact(2) finishes 2 × 1, then fact(3) finishes 3 × 2. The newest box always finishes first.

rows.lua:
local function fact(n)
  if n == 1 then return 1 end
  return n * fact(n - 1)
end
rows.note: With local function (or a global function) the name is visible inside its own body, unlike local fact = function ... end; Python's def always is.
Lua does proper tail calls; Python doesn't, so very deep recursion needs a loop instead.

points: Base case: answers directly, no further call. Recursive case: calls itself on a smaller input.
Every call must get closer to the base case, or you get a RecursionError.
Each call has its own box on the call stack; the newest finishes first.
Work before the call happens on the way in; work after it happens on the way out.
Sums start from a base case of 0; products from 1.
Every path must return its result.
referenceCard.title: Recursion

subtitle: A function that calls a smaller version of itself, until a base case answers directly.

teach.body: Some problems contain a smaller copy of themselves. 3 × 2 × 1 is 3 times (2 × 1). So fact(n) can be n * fact(n - 1). That's the recursive case. It needs a stopping point that answers directly, the base case: fact(1) is 1. Every recursive call must move closer to the base case.
teach.title: Solve a smaller version

teach.body:
When fact(3) calls fact(2), fact(3) isn't finished. Its box stays on the call stack, waiting, with its own n = 3. The newest box is always on top and always the one running. When the base case returns, the boxes come off one at a time, newest first, each finishing its own multiplication. Last in, first out: the call stack is a stack (the SWE track's stack lesson, swe-course-stack-v1, uses the same idea on purpose).

For strings and lists: s[0] is the first item and s[1:] is everything after it.
teach.title: The call stack does the remembering

teach.body: No base case, or calls that never reach it (n + 1 instead of n - 1, or a step that jumps over it), means the boxes pile up until Python stops with a RecursionError. A wrong base case value spreads to every answer: a product whose base case returns 0 is always 0. And every path has to return its result, or the call above gets None.
